progression.startsWith: The stockroom has a bottle of unknown liquid. All you know is that each molecule contains carbon, hydrogen and one oxygen atom. You can't put one molecule on a balance. But a mass spectrometer does something cleverer. It breaks molecules into charged pieces and weighs every piece. The pattern of those masses is a mass spectrum, and each peak can rule possible structures out.
progression.stopsAfter: reading the molecular ion, mass gaps, the base peak and a halogen isotope pair; stating what remains possible.

teaching.task: An unknown liquid contains carbon, hydrogen and one oxygen per molecule. How can breaking its molecules into charged pieces, and weighing each piece, narrow down which structure it has?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) breaking molecules and weighing the charged pieces gives a pattern (1); (2) electrons knock an electron off, fields steer only ions, lighter ions bend more, neutral pieces are not seen (2); (3) m/z reads as mass for 1+ ions; relative abundance (3); (4) the molecular ion leads the cluster at the right, giving the molecular mass; the "one O" condition gives C4H8O; the M+1 bump is the same structure with one carbon-13 (4); (5) isomers share that mass, so the molecular ion can't separate them (5); (6) a bond breaks; the charged piece is detected, the neutral piece is not; the gap is the mass lost (6); (7) common gaps, and 29's two meanings (7); (8) the base peak is the tallest, set to 100%, often a stable fragment, and not the molecular ion (8); (9) butanone's fragments fit both sides of its C=O; fits, not proved (9); (10) chlorine and bromine isotope pairs (10); (11) what MS can't show (11); memory aid (12); attempts (13 to 16); decision rule and handoff (17); key notes (18).
teaching.conversationalApproach: The stockroom has a bottle of unknown liquid. Here's how it weighs them. The detector's counts become a bar chart. Here's the spectrum of our unknown. But a mass of seventy-two doesn't finish the job. Inside the instrument, many molecular ions carry so much energy that a bond breaks. Some gaps turn up again and again. Now look at the tallest peak. Let's read the pieces. Some elements leave a signature. So what has the spectrum told us? The molecular ion gave the mass. Here's a line to remember: find the molecular ion cluster, and tallest is the base. Your turn. Eighty-six minus fifty-seven is twenty-nine, so an ethyl group broke off, leaving C two H five C O plus. Last one. The molecular ion is at ninety-four: the molecule containing bromine seventy-nine. So, when you meet a mass spectrum, work in this order.
teaching.openingDecision: The stockroom has a bottle of unknown liquid. All you know is that each molecule contains carbon, hydrogen and one oxygen atom. You can't put one molecule on a balance. But a mass spectrometer does something cleverer. It breaks molecules into charged pieces and weighs every piece. The pattern of those masses is a mass spectrum, and each peak can rule possible structures out.
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "The mass spectrum shown is of one of two isomers, pentan-2-one or pentan-3-one (molar mass 86 g mol⁻¹). The base peak is at m/z = 57 and there is a strong peak at m/z = 29. Identify the compound. Justify your answer with reference to the fragments." The card shows the pentan-3-one spectrum (Numbers to verify) and the two names; no structures (students draw them from c01). Answer: pentan-3-one. 86 − 57 = 29, loss of C2H5, leaving C2H5CO⁺; pentan-3-one has an ethyl group on both sides of its C=O, so either break gives 57, and 29 is C2H5⁺; pentan-2-one would give a large 43 (CH3CO⁺, after loss of C3H7) and a 71 (after loss of CH3). Crossed mistake: "loss of 29 is CHO, so it's an aldehyde" (neither candidate has a CHO group; check which piece each candidate can lose). (A2, Revision 2) "The mass spectrum of an organic compound shows two peaks of about equal height at m/z = 94 and m/z = 96, and a peak at m/z = 15. Naturally occurring bromine is about 51% bromine-79 and 49% bromine-81. Identify the molecular ion peak, explain the peak at m/z = 96, and identify the fragment responsible for the peak at m/z = 15." The card shows the bromomethane spectrum (measured heights pending, Numbers to verify). Answer: M⁺ at 94 (CH₃⁷⁹Br); 96 is its M+2 partner, the same structure with ⁸¹Br, about as tall because the two isotopes are about equally common; 94 − 15 = 79, loss of a Br atom, leaving CH₃⁺; consistent with bromomethane. Crossed mistake: "96 is the molecular ion, because it's the furthest right" (pre-design trap: isotope peak mistaken for the parent).
teaching.curriculumScope:
Syllabus dotpoint (as printed; NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, p58; C8-IQ2-02 is this project's local catalogue ID, not a code printed in the syllabus), quoted from ../../programme/syllabus/chem-2017-y12.json:

"investigate the processes used to analyse the structure of simple organic compounds addressed in the course, including but not limited to:
- proton and carbon-13 NMR
- mass spectrometry
- infrared spectroscopy (ACSCH130)"

design.visualSystem: spectra are coded only (new stick-spectrum part; never an AI image of a spectrum); spectrum data are realistic for the named compound and listed under "Numbers to verify" for checking against NIST or SDBS; the instrument is painted plates (one existing exterior, one new cutaway); no people, hands or faces; molecules coded in the c08 structure style; at most about three bright text items, earlier lines dim; one reasoning stage at a time; "Pause here to answer." then a 10 s countdown with the full worded question and its spectrum kept on screen; no givens card, givens underlined in the feedback as they are used; brief feedback (answer, key reason, one crossed mistake, about 15 to 30 s); original HSC-style questions only; Australian spelling; no em dashes; conversational narration; no absolute claims ("usually", "fits", "points to", "narrows").
design.transitionPlan: heading writes on: "What do the pieces weigh?". the exterior plate cross-fades to the new m8-ms-cutaway-v1. the cutaway shrinks to a thumbnail at top right. the butanone stick spectrum (Numbers to verify) draws bar by bar from left to right, all bars teal, no labels yet. the candidate strip fills: butanone, butanal, 2-methylpropanal and but-3-en-2-ol as coded skeletal structures, each with a small "72" chip (grey chip "c02: isomers"). right card: break-and-weigh on a generic coded chain "M⁺": it snaps; the left piece gains "+" and drops onto a teal bar (tag "fragment ion: detected"); the right piece greys and floats up with a "?" mass chip (tag "neutral piece: not detected"). the right card becomes a four-row table, each row writing as spoken: "15: CH₃", "17: OH", "29: C₂H₅ or CHO", "45: COOH", each with a tiny coded fragment drawing. the table shrinks to the right edge. gap bracket 72 to 43 with chip "− 29: C₂H₅ or CHO" (bright); then gap bracket 72 to 57 with chip "− 15: CH₃" (the first bracket dims). the board clears to the chloromethane stick spectrum (Numbers to verify). the butanone spectrum returns small at left. the board clears. the board clears. the card stays, shrunk to the top. question card, worded as printed (A2 under Decisions), including the full isotope sentence ("about 51% bromine-79 and 49% bromine-81"). the card stays, shrunk to the top. the board clears. Heading on screen: "Key notes: what to write in your book".
